# Question 1: Expected value

Consider the random variable $X$ characterized by the following PMF.

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
|----:|-------:|
| -1  | .3     |
| 2   | .2     |
| 3   | .5     |

**(1a)** Compute $\textrm{E}[X]$. Show your work.

**Answer:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{E}[X] &= \sum_x x f(x) \\
&= -1 \times .3 + 2 \times .2 + 3 \times .5 \\
&= 1.6
\end{aligned}
$$

**(1b)** Write an R function to compute the expectation of any discrete random variable. The arguments to your function should include the values the random variable can take on (`x`) and the probability it takes on each value (`probs`). Use your function to confirm your answer from question (1a).

**Answer:**

```{r}
exp_func <- function(x, probs){
  sum(x * probs)
}

exp_func(x = c(-1, 2, 3), probs = c(.3, .2, .5))
```

**(1c)** Compute the MSE ($\textrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$) for $c = 0$ and $c = 1$. Show your work.

**Answer:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{E}[(X - 0)^2] &= \sum_x (x - 0)^2 f(x) \\
&= (-1)^2 \times .3 + (2)^2 \times .2 + (3)^2 \times .5 \\
&= 1 \times .3 + 4 \times .2 + 9 \times .5 \\
&= 5.6
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{E}[(X - 1)^2] &= \sum_x (x - 1)^2 f(x) \\
&= (-1 - 1)^2 \times .3 + (2 - 1)^2 \times .2 + (3 - 1)^2 \times .5 \\
&= 4 \times .3 + 1 \times .2 + 4 \times .5 \\
&= 3.4
\end{aligned}
$$

# Question 2: Variance

Consider the random variable $X$ characterized by the following PMF:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
|----:|-------:|
| 0   | .6     |
| 1   | .1     |
| 2   | .3     |

**(2a)** Confirm that the variance of $X$ is the same whether we compute it by the formula in Definition 2.1.12 or the Alternative Formula in Theorem 2.1.13. (We want the two variance computations, not the proof.)

**Answer:** First we calculate $\textrm{E}[X]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{E}[X] &= \sum_x x f(x) \\
&= 0 \times .6 + 1 \times .1 + 2 \times .3 \\
&= .7
\end{aligned}
$$

Using Definition 2.1.12:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{V}[X] &= \textrm{E}\left[(X - \textrm{E}[X])^2\right] \\
&= \textrm{E}\left[(X - .7)^2\right] \\
&= (-.7)^2 \times .6 + .3^2 \times .1 + 1.3^2 \times .3 \\
&= .81
\end{aligned}
$$

To use Theorem 2.1.13, we calculate $\textrm{E}[X^2]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{E}[X^2] &= \sum_x x^2 f(x) \\
&= 0 \times .6 + 1 \times .1 + 4 \times .3 \\
&= 1.3
\end{aligned}
$$

Using Theorem 2.1.13:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{V}[X] &= \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2 \\
&= 1.3 - .7^2 \\
&= .81
\end{aligned}
$$

**(2b)** Write an R function to compute the variance of any discrete random variable. The arguments to your function should include the values the random variable can take on (`x`) and the probability it takes on each value (`probs`). Use your function to confirm your answer from question (2a).

**Answer:**

```{r}
# two versions, both of which use the expectation function I wrote above

# this version uses the E[(X - E[X])^2] formulation
var_func2 <- function(x, probs){
  ex <- exp_func(x, probs)
  exp_func((x - ex)^2, probs)
}

# this version uses the E[X^2] - E[X]^2 formulation
var_func <- function(x, probs){
  exp_func(x^2, probs) - exp_func(x, probs)^2
}

# confirming equality
var_func(x = c(0, 1, 2), probs = c(.6, .1, .3))
var_func2(x = c(0, 1, 2), probs = c(.6, .1, .3))
```

**(2c)** Explain what definition/property/mathematical operation is being used in each step of the following proof.

For random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\textrm{V}[X + c] = \textrm{V}[X]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{V}[X + c] &= \textrm{E}\left[(X + c - \textrm{E}[X + c])^2\right] && \text{(Step 1)} \\
&= \textrm{E}\left[(X + c - \textrm{E}[X] - c)^2\right] && \text{(Step 2)} \\
&= \textrm{E}\left[(X - \textrm{E}[X])^2\right] && \text{(Step 3)} \\
&= \textrm{V}[X] && \text{(Step 4)}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Answer:**

In Step 1, we use the definition of variance applied to the random variable $X + c$.

In Step 2, we use the linearity of expectations and the fact that the expectation of a constant $c$ is $c$.

In Step 3, we simplify by observing that $c - c = 0$.

In Step 4, we use the definition of variance.

# Answer key (practice exercises)

**(P1)** $.2 + .5 + .3 = 1$, and every probability is between 0 and 1, so it's valid.

**(P2)** $\textrm{E}[Y] = 1 \times .2 + 4 \times .5 + 6 \times .3 = .2 + 2 + 1.8 = 4$

**(P3)**

```{r}
exp_func(x = c(1, 4, 6), probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
```

**(P4)**

$\textrm{E}[(Y - 3)^2] = (1-3)^2 \times .2 + (4-3)^2 \times .5 + (6-3)^2 \times .3 = .8 + .5 + 2.7 = 4$

$\textrm{E}[(Y - 4)^2] = (1-4)^2 \times .2 + (4-4)^2 \times .5 + (6-4)^2 \times .3 = 1.8 + 0 + 1.2 = 3$

$c = 4$ has the smaller MSE. That makes sense because $4 = \textrm{E}[Y]$, and the mean is the guess that minimizes MSE.

**(P5)**

```{r}
exp_func(x = (c(1, 4, 6) - 3)^2, probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
exp_func(x = (c(1, 4, 6) - 4)^2, probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
```

**(P6)**

Definition: $\textrm{E}[(Y - 4)^2] = 3$ (this is exactly the second calculation in P4).

Shortcut: $\textrm{E}[Y^2] = 1 \times .2 + 16 \times .5 + 36 \times .3 = .2 + 8 + 10.8 = 19$, so $\textrm{V}[Y] = 19 - 4^2 = 3$.

**(P7)**

```{r}
var_func(x = c(1, 4, 6), probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
var_func2(x = c(1, 4, 6), probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
```

**(P8)** Adding 10 shifts the mean by 10 but doesn't change the spread: $\textrm{E}[Y + 10] = 14$ and $\textrm{V}[Y + 10] = 3$.

```{r}
exp_func(x = c(1, 4, 6) + 10, probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
var_func(x = c(1, 4, 6) + 10, probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
```

**(P9)** $\textrm{V}[2Y] = 2^2 \times 3 = 12$.

```{r}
var_func(x = c(1, 4, 6) * 2, probs = c(.2, .5, .3))
```

**(P10)** Variance is defined as $\textrm{E}[(Y - \textrm{E}[Y])^2]$, which is just the MSE formula $\textrm{E}[(Y - c)^2]$ with the guess $c$ set to the mean. So the variance is the average squared miss when you make the best possible guess.
